name: Esther Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week starts with a primary teaching lecture on how children learn to read, then I'm in school on Wednesdays for placement, in a Year 2 class. Evenings I work at the children's library, three shifts a week, putting on story time and re-shelving. I'm in a flat with two girls from my course. My parents split up when I was twelve, so I spend holidays at Dad's and Mum's, and I'm tired of packing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the classroom days. A six-year-old who finally reads a whole sentence is my favourite thing. What wears me out is writing up lesson plans, which take me twice as long as everyone else. And the sense that everyone in my family has an opinion about whether teaching is a good career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, though I wouldn't make a big thing of it. In schools, it'll be a slightly better way to make worksheets. I'd tell my flatmates that we'll still need teachers who know how to talk to a child who's upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit uneasy, because teaching has its own problems already: pay that doesn't keep up, lots of paperwork, and half the teachers I met on placement want to leave. And my mum's office job is already getting squeezed by software that does her filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the library. I'd keep up my teaching placement diary and ask my mentor teacher to show me how she plans. I'd try one or two of the lesson-planning tools, as long as other student teachers use them too. And I'd save a little from my library pay, about thirty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of a sigh. It's fine, but fine isn't exciting. I'd feel like I'm signing up for a long marathon with no water stations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you try those tools only if others do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you try those tools only if others do?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about teaching as a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not a first adopter. I'd rather someone else finds out if it gives wrong facts, because in a classroom a wrong fact goes to thirty children. If my mentor says a tool's good, I'll try it. If my course mates use it and it saves them an evening, I'm in.

say: I'd say it's a **relief**, but I wouldn't make a big thing of it.
I'd tell my flatmates we'll still need teachers who can talk to an **upset child**.
think: Teaching already has **its own problems**: pay, paperwork and teachers who want to leave.
Mum's office job is already **squeezed** by software that does her filing.
do: **Keep** my degree work and my library shifts, and **ask** my mentor to show me how she plans.
**Try** a lesson-planning tool once other student teachers use it.
**Save** thirty pounds a month from library pay.
feel: A **sigh**: fine but not exciting, like a long marathon with no water stations.
S0.quote: I'd rather someone else finds out if it gives wrong facts, because in a classroom a wrong fact goes to thirty children.
fieldNote: Esther's unease is **old pressure** (pay, paperwork, mum's job), not AI.
Her **steady** stance: adopt once peers or a mentor vouch for a tool.
She frames risk in **classroom terms**: wrong facts reach thirty children.

steps.text: Keep the three weekly library shifts
Try a lesson planning tool once course mates use it
Save thirty pounds a month from library pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change what's taught but not why we teach. Some of it is dull, like marking spelling tests, and I'd happily see that go. But I'd want a rule that nobody replaces classroom teachers with an app to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm in two minds. Schools might use these tools for planning, and that means fewer teaching assistants and maybe fewer jobs for new teachers. And Mum is an office administrator, which is just the kind of job that gets squeezed. Dad is a plumber, so he's safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools in a small way, for example to make differentiated worksheets, and I'd check every one by hand. I'd ask my tutors how they plan to teach us about this, because nobody has told us. I'd also encourage Mum to take an evening course. And I'd keep the library job in case teaching posts dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit wobbly, but I'd manage. It feels like a tide going out: you can't see how far, but you can check the water each day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want teachers to be told about these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want teachers to be told about these tools?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mum do about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which parts they should always do themselves, such as talking to children about feelings, and which parts are fine to hand over. Right now every school is guessing. I'd want a short, honest guide, written by teachers, not by companies, and I'd want training in work time, not on a Sunday night.

say: I'd say it will change **what's taught**, not why we teach, but no app should replace teachers to save money.
I'd happily see **marking** spelling tests go.
think: Schools may need **fewer** teaching assistants and fewer jobs for new teachers.
Mum is an office administrator, a job that gets **squeezed**, while Dad the plumber is safer.
do: **Use** AI tools in small ways, like differentiated worksheets, and check every sheet.
**Ask** my tutors how they plan to teach us about these tools.
**Encourage** Mum to take an evening course and keep my library job.
feel: **Wobbly** but manageable, like a tide going out.
S1.quote: I'd want a short, honest guide, written by teachers, not by companies, and I'd want training in work time, not on a Sunday night.
fieldNote: The **mood** shifts because Mum's office job and fewer teaching posts are both realistic.
She wants **teachers' voices**, not company guides, to decide what is handed over.
Her **steady** habit: use the tools small and check by hand.

steps.text: Make differentiated worksheets with an AI tool and check them by hand
Ask my tutors how the course will teach this
Encourage Mum to start an evening course
Keep the library job in case teaching posts dry up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough time for a school system to react, and teachers should be at the table when the decisions are made. I'd say it quietly, because I'm a first-year and nobody will ask me, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared for the whole family. Mum's office job would go by 2028, and Dad's plumbing would be safe until about 2031 but pay less if fewer people can afford repairs. And I'd be thinking about whether there will be classes of children, or classes run by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to both parents together, which is hard, to see who can help with what. I'd take more library shifts and look for tutoring work, and I'd ask the university about the hardship fund. I'd also stay with the teaching degree because there's something human in it, and I'd learn how to use the tools in lessons so I'm not behind. I wouldn't drop out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened in a quiet way. I'd have a lump in my throat when I walk into a classroom, because I'd wonder if I'm training for something that won't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel to sit both parents down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would it feel to sit both parents down?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hardship fund cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. They haven't been in a room together without lawyers for years, so I'd do it on the phone, three of us. I'd tell my parents I'm not asking for money, I'm asking for a plan. I think they'd both surprise me, because they'd do anything to keep me out of debt.

say: I'd say two years is **not enough** time for schools, and teachers should be at the table.
I'd say it quietly, as a first-year nobody will ask, but I'd **say it**.
think: Mum's office job would go by **2028**, and Dad's plumbing would pay less if repairs fall.
I'd wonder if classes will be run by **software**, not people.
do: **Hold** a three-way phone call with both parents about a plan.
**Take** more library shifts and look for tutoring work.
**Ask** the university about the hardship fund and learn the tools for lessons.
feel: **Frightened** in a quiet way, with a lump in my throat in the classroom.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents I'm not asking for money, I'm asking for a plan.
fieldNote: Mum's job loss within two years plus Dad's **falling repair work** makes this alarmed.
Divorce makes the **family conversation** hard, and she plans it anyway.
She does not drop out; she keeps the human side of teaching as her **anchor**.

steps.text: Phone both parents together to agree a money plan
Take extra library shifts and find tutoring work
Ask the university about its hardship fund
Learn to use AI tools in lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a serious warning, and teaching degrees should add AI skills now, not in the final year. I'd say it to my course reps, because that's where I can actually change something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel anxious but less than the two-year picture. I'd qualify in 2029 and have two years before robots reach hands-on work. Classrooms are hands-on, so I'd probably have a job. My worry would be Mum's office role, which would be gone before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and learn the tools properly on placements. I'd look for a job at a school with a good reputation for support. I'd help Mum look at retraining, perhaps into a school support role, since she's good with children. And I'd save a bit of each library pay so there's a buffer if the school job market shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Some days it feels like an adventure and some days it feels like a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell a child's parent who asks if teachers will be needed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you tell a child's parent who asks if teachers will be needed?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if the warning were two years instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, because children don't learn by themselves, and kids need someone to notice when they're having a bad day. A machine can mark a sentence, but it can't see who didn't eat breakfast. I think that's what teachers are for, and I'd be telling myself as much as them.

say: I'd say five years is a **serious warning** and teaching degrees should add AI skills now.
I'd say it to my **course reps**, where I can change something.
think: I'd qualify in 2029 with **two years** before robots reach hands-on work, and classrooms are hands-on.
Mum's office job would be gone **before** then.
do: **Learn** the tools properly on placements and finish my degree.
**Help** Mum look at retraining into a school support role.
**Save** a bit from each library pay as a buffer.
feel: **Mixed**: some days an adventure, some days a countdown.
S3.quote: A machine can mark a sentence, but it can't see who didn't eat breakfast.
fieldNote: Esther believes the **human side** of teaching lasts, yet the household income side keeps her anxious.
The time lets her act through **course reps** and placements.
Her answer to parents is also a **pep talk to herself**.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools properly during teaching placements
Help Mum research school support role courses
Save a little from each library pay
Raise AI skills with my course reps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the best thing teachers can do is shape how schools use it. I'd say to my future colleagues that we should write the rules before someone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel almost fine. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine and in my seventh year of teaching. Robots might be arriving in classrooms, but I'd have had time to see what they can and can't do. Mum would be close to retirement, so her office job matters less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train as planned and aim to be good at the human parts, like reading, behaviour and kids with extra needs, which software finds hard. I'd learn the tools on the job. I'd also keep a rainy-day fund and pay into the teachers' pension early. And I'd think about a master's in special needs by about 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of curiosity. It's nice to think of myself as someone who gets to see how it plays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would change that calm?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you had a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If funding for schools fell, I'd worry. Machines aren't the only thing that can make a school cut staff. A budget letter can do it too. Then I'd move towards tutoring or a private school, and I'd keep my options open.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough for teachers to **shape** how schools use it.
I'd tell future colleagues to **write the rules** before someone else does.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine in my **seventh year** of teaching, having seen what robots can do.
Mum would be near **retirement**, so her office job matters less.
do: **Train** as planned and get good at reading, behaviour and extra needs.
**Pay** into the teachers' pension early and keep a rainy-day fund.
**Consider** a master's in special needs by about 2032.
feel: Pretty **calm** with a bit of curiosity.
S4.quote: Machines aren't the only thing that can make a school cut staff. A budget letter can do it too.
fieldNote: Esther is **calm about AI** but names school budgets as the more realistic threat.
A decade lets her pick a **specialism**, a steady, planned response.
Mum's near-retirement means the **household worry** fades.

steps.text: Qualify and build skills in reading and behaviour
Pay into the teachers' pension from my first job
Plan a special needs master's for about 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It takes my mum's job and leaves school systems unprepared, while I'd still be in the first half of my degree. What would help is a clear pathway for student teachers on how to work with these tools, real support for people whose office jobs disappear, and schools keeping their staff numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the human side of teaching is the part people forget when they talk about these changes. It's the thing I'm training for, and I hope it counts.

headlineQuote: The human side of teaching is the part people forget when they talk about these changes.
portrait: Esther is **nineteen**, a first-year primary teaching student who works at a children's library and shares a flat with two course mates.
She is **centrist** and steady, trying tools once a mentor or peers vouch for them.
Her parents are divorced: her mum is an **office administrator** and her dad a plumber, so household worries are real.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at the two-year warning, with the human side of teaching as her anchor.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, taking Mum's job while schools are unprepared.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **pathway** for student teachers on AI tools, support for displaced office workers and steady school staffing.
